title: Comparison
description: The relation between two assessments, and the only place a diff belongs. A diff is not part of an assessment: it is a claim about two states, and putting it inside one would make that state carry an assertion about another. This may be cached, exported or shipped inside a delivery package, and it stays derivable in all three cases: given both assessments, the engine reproduces it.

$schema.description: The exact contract this document claims, which must be the $id of the schema validating it. An instance convention and not the dialect keyword: inside a schema document `$schema` names the JSON Schema dialect, and using one field for both meanings is what this separation exists to prevent. It replaces `schema_version`, which was a second version that could not even express the one in the $id — `1.0` against a contract ending in `/1.2.0` — and was maintained by hand.

side.description: Which assessment, by identity rather than by copy. A comparison that embedded both would duplicate the canonical truth it is describing.

tenant.description: Which tenant both sides are about, copied from the assessments rather than restated. It was a bare string, which put a hostname where an organisation belongs.

canonical_hash.description: The assessment's canonical digest. Identity that can be verified rather than trusted, and the reason a comparison never carries a path: a path says where a file sat on one machine, not what it held.

produced_by.description: The engine version that computed it. A diff nobody can reproduce is an opinion about history.

resource.description: The resource whose finding moved, as a reference rather than a string two documents had to spell identically.

kind.description: What happened to this resource-and-rule pair between the two sides. Three values because there are only three, and for `added` and `removed` the kind is already the complete observation: there is no earlier state that could have moved.

changes.description: What was OBSERVED to differ, and never why. These were called causes, which claimed something the engine cannot know: when evidence and the rule move together, saying which one produced the new outcome needs a counterfactual evaluation that nobody ran. A changed outcome is itself an observation, not an explanation of one.

attribution.description: Optional, and absent until somebody actually evaluates causality. Kept apart from `changes` so that observing several things move together never reads as knowing which one mattered. Under `ambiguous`, factors are candidates rather than confirmed causes, and the state is what says so.

state.description: `ambiguous` is a real answer and probably the common one: two things moved and the comparison cannot separate them. `not-evaluated` says nobody tried, which is a different sentence. `established` is a claim, and a claim carries what and how or it is not one.

factors.description: What the attribution points at. `outcome` is deliberately not a value: the outcome is the effect, and listing it here would put the result among its own causes.

method.description: How it was established. Re-evaluating the older evidence against the newer rule is a method; noticing that both moved is not.

outcome.description: Five states, never three, and `null` where the side did not carry this pair at all.
